576.t: Laid off after 21 years and never looking back
576.s: She was laid off at 58 with a year's severance, then worked full time as a musician ever since.
576.q: like so — how do they do this to me you know, after I worked here all these 21 years and oh my God and feeling sorry for myself and the whole trip. You know what? I had prayed that I would be able to start singing more. And be careful what you pray for, you might get it. And you know what? I never…

576.t: Being laid off at 58 and singing full-time
576.s: Laid off from the advertising agency at 58 with a year's severance, she went out as a singer, prayed for more singing, and has worked more ever since.
576.q: Yeah, we have. You know, actually I‟ve been working. When I got laid off from my job when I was 58 years old, I cried. I was worried. How am I gonna support myself? Brown, C.: The best thing that ever happened to you.

576.t: Keeping a day job and supporting the music
576.s: She kept an office job to support her daughter and keep the music pure, and sang jazz jingles for the advertising agency.
576.q: Yeah. I think so, for me I would say yes. I never thought of myself as a part time singer because I didn’t do it full time. I worked in an office for two reasons. I had a daughter to support, I didn’t want her raised the way I was raised as a young kid which was in a very, very poverty stricken…

514.t: Art Tatum and Lucky Roberts and day jobs as a way of life
514.s: Earlier musicians also held day jobs and played the real music at after-hours sessions.
514.q: Yeah. Art Tatum I think worked at the library. He would play his gig. The gig was just a means to the end but the real music would come to the after night sessions. He would go for the sessions. I wasn’t here but this is what I was told. Lucky Roberts played and jammed all night where they would…

514.t: Messenger jobs, Milt Hinton's respect, other musicians' day jobs
514.s: He tells of Milt Hinton seeing him deliver papers and Mona Hinton's later words, and lists musicians like McCoy Tyner and Bob Cranshaw with day jobs.
514.q: After taxes. And this was before the bikes came in. I was a messenger. I was taking the subway and walking. Package was fifty cents then. Then my big job came after that, I worked with the Wall Street Journal I had two bags of newspapers. I’d get there at six o’clock in the morning and pack up my…

514.t: Lean times around 1967-68 and day jobs before Lee Morgan's call
514.s: Work was tight so he took a job at Alexander's, and each time he took a day job a gig, like Lee Morgan's, came.
514.q: Oh well I can tell you precisely. I think, let me see now, it could have been around maybe close to ’68, ’67, ’68. Things were getting a little tight so I would always say well it’s no point in me waiting for the phone to ring so. So I said let me see what I can find. Now mind you playing music all…

244.t: Caterpillar career and continuing to gig
244.s: He became a tool room machinist over 36 years while playing casual gigs.
244.ch: Day jobs and Bay Area gigs
244.q: Well, played what you call gigs around casual engagement. Other than the regular we had at the Sweets Barroom. And I played with, you know, the little gigs around.

244.t: WPA, shoe shop jobs and Caterpillar
244.s: He worked on WPA, then shoe repair, then Caterpillar from 1942, while gigging at Sweets Ballroom with Ben Watkins.
244.ch: Day jobs and Bay Area gigs
244.q: then I started on the WPA I got a job on the WPA at the last minute I said well I can't make it here well you out of the you are doing pretty good with your eyes so I think I'll go to Chicago I had friends that in Chicago that was the late Joey DeRiley he was a drummer on the band and the late…

246.t: Playing with Johnny Predoss's Camellia band at the 1950 storm
246.s: Glass says he was with Johnny Predoss's Camellia band in 1950 and men hired him when Johnny had no work.
246.q: We were Johnny Predoss. That's in 1950. Yeah, the Camellia band. I was playing with the Camellia band. And you must have stayed with them for a while. I did stay with Johnny. I stayed with Johnny. Those used to work from one place to the other, from one band to the other. Fellas would hire me when…

246.t: Depression years unloading rail cars and playing picnics
246.s: During the Depression Glass worked for himself unloading gondola and gravel cars for little pay and played music when asked.
246.q: I was playing for myself in the Depression. I was working for myself. I'd get out there and work and unload cold cars. I'd catch a job playing, go to the lake or something like that, you know? And I'd play them picnics. You still unload them cold cars? I'd unload gondola cars by myself. I unload…

248.t: Leaving full-time music for the Whitney Bank
248.s: Dawson says he took a job at the Whitney Bank in 1917 and kept playing night jobs.
248.q: Well I was practicing with Rene and then after the storm in 1915 I went to work, then I went to work at the Whitney Bank. After the crash came about and things got bad, you know, things got dull, so the law came up, I'd work, fight and go to jail. That was around 1917, you see. And so I just got…

248.t: Getting a night job at the Whitney Bank during work-or-fight
248.s: Dodging work-or-fight, Dawson got on the Whitney Bank night staff through a barbershop tip, arranged to leave for gigs, moved to a day job and worked fifty-two years until pensioned.
248.ch: Early life and the Whitney Bank
248.q: I'll tell you how it happened. I was hustling. That time I was a gambler. A lot of ways, that's all I, I didn't do no work or nothing. I'd just catch it what I could. And, uh, running around from district to district. What happened, this colored fellow that worked for the Whitney, he was in a…

903.t: Good paying day jobs and giving up the road
903.s: Clayton recalls well paid jobs at Bramson's and the oil company, but says they do not last and he will not give up music.
903.q: Yeah, that's right. And then I was making good money out there too. My money was a hundred and sixty something dollars a week. Besides my riders I used to carry.

903.t: Music is tough now; last job and Paul the drummer
903.s: Clayton says work is scarce; his last job was a short parade gig and a serenade for his father, and he mentions drummer Paul who plays with him regularly.
903.q: Well I'm going to tell you this, it's really tough. I ain't played a job since I played that little two hour job on a parade that's, when was that? The Southern School? Yeah, the Southern School, yeah, that's right.

619.t: Letter carrier in 1919 and earnings at the roofing trade
619.s: He carried mail for eighteen months, quit in 1919 for the roofing trade, whose pay rose far past the post office's, and he now owns rental property.
619.ch: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
619.q: I gave it up. Went back to my trade. In 1919. I scanned mail in 1919. I gave it up. So, I gave 18 months carrying mail and I gave it up. Went back to my trade, which I was doing. So, I was in the post office making 3,020 cents a day. I just raised our salary to $6 a day. You understand? So, I went…

619.t: Working a day trade and playing all night
619.s: He recalls roofing by day, playing until three or four in the morning, and transposing piano copies into parts.
619.ch: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
619.q: On the same job. Night after night. No days off. Yeah, it's hard. Shut up. You shut up all that time. But, you know, some of us get a kick out of it. Like I used to do. I didn't feel like I was working or anything. I used to get my kick out of it.

152.t: Longshoreman, liquor sales and the Glazer job
152.s: Union trouble led him to work three years as a longshoreman, then liquor sales, then drug wholesaler sales until about 1990.
152.q: So my brother, uh, the one that's a little old, that was, uh, ahead of me, he's about four years old, uh, he was working as a longshoreman. I worked as a longshoreman for three years. Um.

152.t: Loading ships on the Puerto Rico boat
152.s: He describes longshoreman work loading flour sacks.
152.q: I, I, I used to, uh, they had a boat out there that used to come, uh, every other Wednesday, every two weeks, called a Puerto Rico boat. Uh huh. Uh huh. We would wake eight hours in a day and 11 hours at night. Hmm.

290.t: Ninth Ward trades, musicians' day jobs and trappers
290.s: Many musicians lived on music alone; Ninth Ward trades and the Moss Pickers and Coon Trappers club.
290.q: Like, the different musicians, did they work days? Well, some of them worked in carpentry business, you know, and some... done some kind of work where they wasn't compelled to go to work every day. Mm-hmm. So, in case they had to stay out at night too late, they'd just be able to stay home.

290.t: Blacksmith day job (and one night on the Capitol boat)
290.s: From age seventeen he worked as a blacksmith with wagons and carriages until retirement; the trade was easier to find than music work and made playing hard. He also substituted once on the Capitol boat.
290.ch: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
290.q: One time in my life, what time. I was called, just I'll tell you, shortage of people, I was called to take the place of a trumpet player. Well he wasn't in all the bands. No, no, no, I just called to do a job one night, one time. I see.

881.t: The Depression, the post office and Eugene Wright's band
881.s: He carried mail while playing with Eugene Wright's young band, and was forced out over holding two jobs.
881.q: Yeah, things didn't straighten out. First I started carrying mail out of the old post office. But I got a little break. There came a call for a trombone player and they didn't know I was an old man and I didn't know these young kids. There was Eugene Wright, Eugene Wright and his Dukes of Swing. So…

881.t: Election commission work and rejoining Franz Jackson
881.s: He does clerical work for the election commission and went back to Franz Jackson's band.
881.q: Do you have any day work? Well, I did some day work last year. I worked at the, well, it's nothing to it. Anytime you see me working well, you know, it's nothing to it. I'm never going to work hard anymore. I'm too old. I'm working at the election commission. Yeah. And it's just a little clerical…

229.s: Blakeney recalls the elder William Woodman as a fast trombonist, and they discuss musicians holding day jobs such as barbering.
229.ch: The Los Angeles music scene in the early 1930s
229.q: was a good musician on the trombone and the articulation, boys followed him and his style, on the trombone. He made a lot of fast passages on the trombone; he was famous for that.

229.t: Working for the Board of Education
229.s: After Burke's band broke up he worked twenty-one years for the Los Angeles school board.
229.ch: C.L. Burke and Kid Ory years
229.q: Well yes, after I started working with Ory, because it was about eight months after I left C.L. before I started with Ory.

769.t: Giving up music in the late 1920s
769.s: Music got tough, his last job was in the Irish Channel, and he sold his drums while continuing night work at the bank.
769.ch: Giving up and returning to music
769.q: That was back in the 20s, late 20s. Well, after that music kind of died down and I gave it up. But I was still doing night work with the National Bank.

709.t: Moving to New Orleans after the 1915 storm; night watchman job
709.s: Kelly came to New Orleans after the 1915 storm. He stopped playing and worked as a night watchman at a lumber yard to raise his children.
709.ch: Early life and the plantation brass band
709.q: And took up and went to work out there, put this big lumber yard out there on the feet in Robinson. We were a media in company. I get to the other boys. Oh yeah. And you see, I was up with that now. Out there. I got to be a night watcher out there. And it was like, you know, I was up with that. And…

724.t: Playing with many bands at once while keeping a day job
724.s: He might work with four bands in a week and kept a day job as stock cutter in a shoe factory.
724.ch: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
724.q: I wanted to ask you something. How many bands would you be playing with at one time? Say you're playing with one guy, Kid Thomas for example, on the weekends. How many other bands would you be working with during the course of the week? Well, like I know, I'm waiting with Kid Thomas. Weekends would…

241.t: Missed Sammy, day jobs and painting
241.s: Talk about a Friday job, Sammy's packing work and his own work painting after being laid off from the railroad.
241.q: When was Sunday? That was Friday. Friday, yeah. Yeah, Friday. We played a Friday. We played at two hours. And, uh... Sammy couldn't make it? Sammy couldn't make it, no. You see, he couldn't make it.

185.t: Other trades: cigar maker uncle, bricklayer father, Louis Nelson
185.s: Uncle Papa was a cigar maker and the father a bricklayer, Louis Nelson may have studied with them, and Lorenzo did nothing but music.
185.q: No, my brother was strictly to music, all his life, he never did anything but music. That's the reason why I made him so famous, he could, there was nothing to music to him, just like drinking a glass of water. Because he never done nothing else in his life but that.

1000.s: Bertrand worked as a first-class waiter and also played piano on the same jobs; he died some years earlier and was a native New Orleanian.
1000.q: Yeah, he used to live on, he used to live around Krause there on, on North Ferry between, let me see now, North Ferry. He's right by Krause there used to live, right across from Krause.

625.t: Work schedule and day jobs during the big-band years
625.s: Trotter says he worked a couple of nights a week with Celestin and Robert Clark and held a grocery job while single; schoolboys filled the bands.
625.q: Well, we'd work long, twice a week. And did you work days then? Well, I had a little job then. It wasn't too much. When I was with Celestan, I didn't work because, well, I was single. And I was just in a band just to say I was, you know, had a lot of publicity then, you know, in the band.

647.t: Post office route, carnival season and the union
647.s: Musicians working day jobs, his mail route, going less often to play and keeping his union membership.
647.ch: Post office, day job and quitting
647.q: Yeah, at one time, yes he was. But now, a lot of those guys, uh, how they do it during the ball carnival season, I don't know how they do it.

83.t: Running a dry cleaning business while keeping the studio
83.s: After Dover failed he ran a large dry cleaning and laundry operation to pay bills, while paying others to run the studio; the interviewer met him then.
83.q: Well, I was forced to. I had to run another business for a couple of years, you know, to make money. So I ran a large dry cleaning and laundry operation.

267.t: Marriage and his day job as a hospital orderly
267.s: Pay from music was too low, so Ford married and worked at Charity Hospital, earning 20 dollars a week in 1951.
267.q: did you have a day journal? Yeah. Oh yeah. First I worked at the charity hospital where my mother just retired from. I was an orderly, an award, and I worked in every phase I believe of the hospital. I was in an accident room a while. I was in an admitting room. Oh wow. I worked, which my mother's…

268.t: Day job with the light company from 1939
268.s: He began with the power company in 1939 and retired after 33 years.
268.ch: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
268.q: I retired June 1st. It was this year. In 33 years.

620.t: When and why he stopped playing
620.s: He says he quit playing, tracing it to stiff hands, riverfront work, jukeboxes, low pay and the new union, while Dejan tries to date it.
620.q: Oh, no. I don't believe I could play no more. I'm playing years. No. In years I played. I could... I don't believe I could play nothing no more.

40.t: Firehouse job and jam sessions with captain and lieutenant
40.s: Zanco is a fireman at Central Station in the French Quarter, with free time. Captain Martin Finity (banjo) and Lieutenant Sidney Del Paget (drums) play with him at the firehouse.
40.q: Well, they had this captain by the name of Martin Finity. He used to be a banjo player years ago. And when I decided to bring my horn around the firehouse one day, he said he would bring his banjo. So between the two of us, we'd worked up a duet. So in the meantime, this other fella, he's a…

601.t: Frankie Duson's job: not a barber, only music
601.s: Russell asks whether Frankie Duson had another job. Tom and Martin say his father was a barber but Frankie never was, and as far as they know he did nothing but music.
601.ch: Algiers places, ball games and Frankie Duson
601.q: He never did a barber. I knew him since I was there. I never knew him to have a job.

41.t: Paul works in the fur business and returns in 1925
41.s: Paul left music around 1923-24 when the Rhythm Kings broke up and worked in the fur business, then returned in 1925 to form the New Orleans Rhythm Kings again.
41.ch: Southland label and the fur business
41.q: he went well he was located here in the 500 block of Decatur and later in the 20s he went on Chapitulas and South Peterson Gravia and Paul worked also the foyer business in those years nearly after he came back from when he gave up music in the 23 24 when the Rhythm Kings broke up and rap got sick…

403.t: Bolden had no other job; Jones's barbering and blindness
403.s: Bolden only played music after school, never barbered. Jones was a barber himself, stopped about 20 years ago and lost his sight.
403.q: Not in my noise. But I know it before I got to be a barber. He didn't, never worked, nobody in my noise. He only played music. After he left school.

799.s: He worked as a welder in a shipyard until two bouts of pneumonia; it was exhausting work.
799.q: Well during the war I got into the shipyard until I got pneumonia twice and I had to give that up. I became a welder. And boy you talk about hard work.

628.s: He and Lawrence worked day jobs at Holtzman's store but always got off in time to play at night.
628.q: Me and Lawrence used to work in the front of the store. Worked for Holtzman at 510 Frenchman Street.

972.t: Day jobs: slater, ice, coffee and the sugar boat
972.s: He describes work as a slater, plasterer and painter, hauling ice and coffee on the river, and his last job as a sugar-boat sweeper in 1957-58.
972.q: Oh, yeah, I used to work, first I used to work for Al Mastricht, 919 on Lobster Street, and I used to do all the slater work, paper hanging, plaster, that's my tray, and I knew that I'd do carbonate work. And I done all that. I went for D'Alandino real estate at 729 Newton Street. I done all that…

432.t: Canal Street gigs and his United Food day job
432.s: He worked Canal Street and kept a day job at United Food Company.
432.ch: Lee Collins and the riverboat Washington
432.q: I worked there a while. See, cause I wouldn't work, you know, like alternate, like, God won't get off two nights or something like that, you know. I'd work like that. All the more penitentiary jobs, I didn't even need the college jobs. That's right, penitentiary. Yeah. I worked on them guys. I used…

482.t: Tuts's current work and plans for a recording
482.s: Tuts says he is playing at a church, was laid off from the Gold Room on St. Charles, and is hunting a winter job; the researcher mentions a German interested in his music.
482.q: Well, right now I ain't doing anything. I'm just working at her church about two weeks now. I'm doing it. Last Thursday is Monday. Now, next Monday I'm going to get out there. She's going to get me to get me to get me. With the band? No, she's going to get her daughter and her cousin. And I'm…

188.t: Cement work and the end of music jobs
188.s: When music jobs got scarce he did cement work, shipping, and dance hall jobs at 25 a week, around 1935, then factory and shipyard jobs.
188.ch: Own band, lake picnics, day jobs
188.q: i got in uh the music got on you know so low you know i got my job on a steamer of course i always did do my cement work in between you know well i didn't know you you worked at cement cement finishing

632.s: Talbert, Joe Watkins and others held daytime jobs such as janitor; George Lewis was a longshoreman.
632.q: Uh... As I remember, Talbert had a cleaning and pressings on it. Uh... Yeah. I think some of them did. Many of them did.

665.t: Working as a night maid at funeral homes
665.s: She worked as nightmaid for undertakers, serving the bereaved, instead of giving parties herself.
665.q: but you can't do that now because people come to your house drunk and cut up. You have to call the law for them. So I don't bother giving nothing like that. I didn't before I got crippled. I'd rather go out and work. I worked at the Undertaker because the people had got too funny.

777.t: Union, railroad insurance and Illinois Central retirement
777.s: He left the union, discusses railroad group insurance, and his 37 years on the Illinois Central ending with a 1956 retirement letter; he took days off to play.
777.ch: Instruments, own band and the Eureka
777.q: No, I got out of the union. But now I wouldn't get back. I wouldn't go back, but you can't get the death part, so I wouldn't get the death part. No, see, I didn't pass the age.

570.s: Penn has worked for Security Storage for fourteen years after about ten at OK Storage, and discusses when he married.
570.q: Well, what I did, you see, I got... By the time I got married I went and got a job, because I used to work. I remember playing music, you see.

139.t: Work as a cement finisher and mechanic
139.s: He describes his trade as cement finishing, learned from Bo Brothers after the service in 1945, plus carpentry and truck repair.
139.q: I learned that on the job. And then I did all that job then I worked for myself.

284.t: His day job at the pressing shop
284.s: He worked part-time pressing clothes three days a week.
284.q: Well, I happened not to be working then. I had a job, but it was a part-time job. I was pressing, real pressing shop. And I only worked three days a week. And that was on the corner of Royal and Espanol.

878.t: Day jobs: house painting and railroad electrician
878.s: Harry, Jim and Larry painted houses; Larry sold church goods, and Harry worked for a railroad as an electrician.
878.q: Did Larry do any outside work when he was a kid? Larry was a house painter, yeah. He was too. Of course, Larry was a salesman too. Mm-hmm. He sold church goods, and...

8.t: Brother Johnny Garland and day jobs versus music
8.s: His brother Johnny played with no particular band and advised never letting music interfere with a job; a comparison with a blueprint man.
8.ch: New Orleans bands, brass bands and learning bass
8.q: Who did he play with? Johnny didn't play with any particular person. When he was here. Because he said he never let music interfere with a job. He tried to teach me that. Always keep a job. It would depend on music. I couldn't see it that way. Oh, music. He was a blueprint. Which kind of?…

571.t: Riverfront work: PWA job, coffee sacks and boosting
571.s: Alongside music, Lewis worked on the riverfront from about 1937, mostly with coffee. He explains the three-man boosting method, the counting rhythm, and the wrist injury from lifting too soon.
571.ch: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
571.q: During that time, I was working for the PWA. I had to get up at six o'clock in the morning and catch the bus and work until two in the evening. And then I'd come home and sleep and I'd meet this job. I started at the riverfront around 37.

635.t: Day jobs: coal wagon alongside Louis Armstrong and long-shore work
635.s: Foster and Louis both drove coal wagons; he held several day jobs while playing every night.
635.ch: Youth and day jobs in New Orleans
635.q: So you told me about that. Well, Tennessee coal company and I waited for the Pittsburgh coal company. See. And we used to meet. I'd buy her the whisker. See, I was for uptown coal company. But I'd be delivering coal downtown and he's coming uptown to us. So we'll meet over here and we'll wait. This…

176.s: He worked many spots on Decatur Street near the river.
176.q: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Were you된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 I work in a lot of them spots…

968.t: Lumber yard and furniture store jobs
968.s: Marrero describes working at a furniture store and a lumber yard on the Industrial Canal before George called him back, and says he has not touched his banjo for a long time.
968.q: Oh, I didn't know. No, out of the lumber yard. Then I left the furniture store, then out of the lumber yard. And I was working hard, too. I was so glad with George come back and met that job.

883.t: Weeks Hall and Frank Doatree's furniture store jobs
883.s: Bunk worked off and on for Weeks Hall and for Frank Doatree's furniture store, where he was also night watchman.
883.q: And he worked for Frank Doatree even then. And then he was a watchman at night at this place when he was building up the new store. And then after… What store was that? Frank Doatree.

831.t: Day jobs and musicians at the McGinnis cotton mill
831.s: Most musicians had day jobs; he worked at the cotton mill alongside other musicians.
831.ch: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
831.q: day jobs sure because there wasn't any music to be played in the daytime they say three-fourths of them i'd say all of them i'd say all of them i'd say all of them had day jobs because you couldn't make any money playing music in the daytime there wasn't no day jobs going around only like on a…

293.t: Lottery vendor job, pension and current playing
293.s: Worked about 36 years as a lottery vendor, is now 68 on a pension, shows his Epiphone banjo and still plays picnic jobs.
293.q: I worked at Lacha for 36 years about. You see now I'm on a pension and everything's over now. Of course I get jobs, little jobs you know what I mean.

196.t: Quitting music for the public service and working the racetrack
196.s: He quit playing around 1923 for 41 years with the public service, retired about 1964, and now works as a mutuel auditor at the fairgrounds.
196.ch: After the music: Army, public service, family
196.q: and went to work for public service I was 41 years there 41 years with the north public service and I retired there about six years ago so I spent practically half my life with with the public service

298.t: George's three jobs and little sleep
298.s: Talk of how a drummer named George juggled theatre, wax museum and music jobs, despite his boss's urging.
298.ch: Fellow musicians and brass band world
298.q: Three and four jobs. That's right. That's right. And he still find time to get in trouble, I mean. Find time to go around all them women's he had. Oh, that man was so good.

909.s: Morris returned to freight handling at the port and stayed, and gave up his truck.
909.q: So they told me they gave me credit for that. See, and I went back at the port and I've been there ever since. Of course, we might get bad, but after all, I'm too glad that I had a place to go to at that time.

801.t: Stopping music in 1928: low pay, marriage, odd jobs
801.s: Eddie says he stopped around 1928 when the pay fell to a dollar, he got a job and married. The sibling clarifies he later played only occasional odd jobs, never a regular band.
801.q: It got rotten. They were playing for a dollar nine. So I had to get a job. I got married. Well my brother, he stood, Lawrence. He stood until he died. All my brothers. I'm not a fun gamer. And uh. Well. We made up the young Tuxedo then. Mm-hmm. Son of a.

476.t: Going to work for the L&N Railroad
476.s: From October 1936 Joe worked for the railroad and drifted away from music; he describes his jobs from Red Cap to the freight depot.
476.q: And uh... Well, let's say I played with uh... Paul Maurice for quite a number of years. I don't know, I went to work for the railroad. And that was in the lower part of 36. 1936, October of the exact. And uh... Somehow or another, I had practically got away from music. So uh... I worked there for…

309.t: Why musicians stay active and his day jobs
309.s: Julius says music is his life; after becoming disabled he did only delivery and heavy warehouse work.
309.q: Well, now, like Sunday, like my neighbors around here Sunday, this guy bored me so with the sacks and I just let him sit there and blew and he blowed and blowed until he blew himself down and he'd sit down. Well, they had a big festival or something they had from St. Bernard Street all around here…

786.t: Scarce work and the police running musicians off the street
786.s: Shade says work has fallen off to scuffling, and that police now stop street playing though they once earned good money in a few hours.
786.q: Oh, been and fell off here. I ain't been doing nothing much. About once every month, just like you said, about once every month, every three months, sometimes twice a week, sometimes no times every week, just everything and went flop. Yeah, ain't nothing here.

433.s: Alkyer says the 2008-09 recession hurt JazzTimes and JazzIz. He now focuses on DownBeat but wants healthy competition.
433.ch: The state of jazz and the magazine business
433.q: I used to when I was younger. And then, and I think it was probably around the 2008, 9, when the big recession hit and you know both of my major U.S. competitors, we can say the names, JazzTimes and JazzIz, they’re friends of mine. JazzIz went dark and was sold and came back out. But they had some…

311.t: Non-music jobs, doing everything well, and retiring from Metropolitan Life
311.s: Menial jobs before the Metropolitan; his father's advice to do everything well earned promotions, and he retired in 1976.
311.q: Shined shoes — red capped down on Third and Townsend where the trains come in, washed windows at the Metropolitan, run an elevator. A lot of menial work.

674.t: Moving to New York and surviving lean times
674.s: He says he fell into the Wonder job, later made it through lean times in the early 90s and never held a lasting non-music job.
674.q: how I was going to do it, you know, so I just like I fell into that Stevie Wonder gig. And the funny thing is I went from one to another and the cost of living was nothing like it is now. God, like I don’t know how people do it now. I mean you’ve certainly got to make a lot of money going out of…

691.t: Day job at King's County Hospital
691.s: Juggling hospital typing work with club gigs until she resigned for out-of-town jobs.
691.q: It was. And my supervisor said, “You have to make a choice.” I was working in King’s County Hospital in Brooklyn in the Student Nurses’ Department typing up the tests and lectures and things. And I was doing a lot of work. And so she said it’s not good for your health and so forth. She was giving…

517.s: The mid-1960s were his leanest years; now things are better than ever.
517.q: Well each year is different. I got — the leanest years, one of my leanest years was for me, was back maybe back in the mid-60’s or something like that. There was a time when there just wasn’t too much happening. Maybe it was just for me, or it could have been for the rest of the industry, I don’t…

1009.t: Dual life as marine biologist and musician in Trinidad
1009.s: In Trinidad he worked as a full-time research biologist while playing music.
1009.q: I was doing as much as a marine research biologist as I was doing as a musician. My life was completely split between music and a full time research appointed job for which I got United Nations fellowships to travel and study. My specialty was in sea floor ecology.

966.s: Davis defines a freelancer as someone with stylistic range who does not rely on one steady job.
966.q: That’s a great question. I mean I think of a freelance player as somebody who basically has the ability and the range stylistically and do a lot of, a wide variety of work. And I think if that’s not the definition that would certainly be a helpful quality if you’re going to be a freelance player.…

539.s: Dorn compares producers to running backs and recalls the early eighties when the business changed and he could not get work. He then ran his own companies.
539.q: Listen, record producers are really like running backs in the NFL. You get your three, four, five years you know? This is 46 years coming up on that I’m doing this. I had a very ugly period in the early eighties, I couldn’t get any work. The music was changing and I was still doing what I did you…

718.t: A working musician's untypical week and creative freedom
718.s: Fedchock says no week is typical; in New York he did everything but wanted to keep creative freedom rather than assembly-line work.
718.q: There really is no typical week. The typical is there’s no typical. It really depends on the time of year, it could be, you know I could be traveling doing something at a school, I could be overseas, I could be home writing, I could be working in Manhattan, I could be just practicing and honing my…

420.s: He describes jobs like his father's sauerkraut factory and floors in Boston.
420.q: Yeah, sure. Not like I didn’t always know that I should be doing this, but different points where you capitulate to existence, and the raw inherently unjust way things are in life. I should be able to do this all the time, and make a whole pile of money, and have a whole bunch of friends, and like…

743.t: Would he do it again, and non-music jobs
743.s: Gordon would choose a musician's life again; he sometimes held non-musical jobs.
743.q: Yes I think I would, yeah.

165.t: Non-music jobs and appreciating music as a living
165.s: Brief talk of paying dues in other jobs before music.
165.ch: Vocalese and Sing a Song of Basie
165.q: I say that’s the period at which my feet touched the ground, you know? Because music keeps you up in the air you know.

694.t: Pub gigs and day jobs on the railway and casual labor
694.s: He describes pub hours, a Carnaby Street bar, working on the railway, and later casual agency labor between gigs.
694.q: Oh sometimes it was that and there was a little bar we used to do near Carnaby Street, it had a pretty grueling night shift you know. It was not quite the same as the Beatles would have been doing in Hamburg but it was enough. But most of the pubs were kind of like

898.t: Non-music jobs: Frontier Airlines and Tower Records
898.s: He only worked summers loading luggage at Frontier Airlines to buy a saxophone and briefly at Tower Records in Boston.
898.q: No. [sound of knock on wood]. No I never have. I’ll tell you, the only thing I would do, in the summers I would work in Denver for Frontier Airlines and I worked this job because I wanted to buy a saxophone. So I loaded planes and loaded luggage and unloaded luggage for I think two summers. And…

808.t: Earlier career as a Cobol programmer
808.s: She used to be a business programmer and now enjoys computers as a user.
808.q: And I still love computers. I don’t program them anymore. I used to program them but I left those days behind, I just use them now. I was a business programmer in the Cobol language. I actually liked it a long time ago, but it’s more fun to just use my Macintosh and use E-mail and all those fun…

749.s: She has worked only in music for fifty years and has no experience of a day job.
749.q: Hmm. I just realized, this is 2023. I’ve been doing this consecutively for fifty years plus now. Okay? And I’ve never done anything but music, anything but music. Even if I were in some acting thing I could sing. You know what I mean? I mean there was a part where you had to sing something, so I…

343.t: Nine years off the stage after Pharoah
343.s: McBee was unable to find work from about 1974 to 1983 and says it made him a better person.
343.q: Well you asked me in the previous talk whether or not I had bumps or periods that prevailed on my arrival in New York. Financially I never really suffered any drama of that. But I did enter a period of nine years, this was right after Pharoah Sanders that I was off the stage for nine years. There…

838.s: After leaving he lost contacts and worked fixing pool tables briefly.
838.q: After I left the Basie band I was fixing pool tables. ‘Cause when anybody would see me on the street they’d say, “Hey man, I didn’t know the band was in town.” When I left the Basie band I’d been in big bands for five years so all contacts and things here — so when I left the band I put on a pair…

349.s: He worked construction, shipping clerk and department store jobs but disliked combining them with gigs.
349.ch: Early gigs and the war years
349.q: Yeah I’ve the daytime, yeah. I’ve worked construction work, I’ve worked as a shipping clerk, I’ve worked, let’s see, department store. That’s about all I can think of right now. But I didn’t really like that so much, working, in one thing and then playing after that. That really didn’t strike up…

396.t: Part-time medical transcribing to leave time to practice
396.s: She did part-time jobs such as medical transcribing, translating and editing so she could practice.
396.q: It wouldn’t work, no. And I was willing to do a series of part time jobs. We were talking about transcribing, and I did many years as a medical transcriber. Anything that — I tried full time work but I just wasn’t able to get any practicing in. So I went to part time jobs that didn’t take a whole…

552.s: Hospital stock clerk, shoe salesman and the dishwashing job he quit for a disco band.
552.ch: Richmond and arriving in New York
552.q: Not in New York. While I was in school I did work a non-music job, I worked in a hospital as a stock clerk on weekends. I had to work every weekend and holidays, which was rough, because a lot of times on holidays you want to go home to visit your family, that kind of thing. So there were times I…

961.t: The only non-music job: draftsman at Hughes Aircraft
961.s: Around 1957, newly married, he spent six months as a draftsman at Hughes Aircraft; otherwise he has worked in music, including shows and strip joints.
961.ch: Making a living: studio and odd work
961.q: Only in the beginning. About 1957 it would have been when I was first married, I worked for about six months at an aircraft plant at Hughes Aircraft in Los Angeles, as a draftsman and industrial artist, which that isn’t even done anymore, it’s all graphic art now. We used to actually use pencils…

618.t: Being both a musician and a physician
618.s: He describes how musicians and doctors each wondered about his commitment, which proved no impediment.
618.q: I think on both sides. Initially very early on some musicians, knowing that I was a physician and I was either studying to become a psychiatrist or after I’d actually become a psychiatrist, might say, “well gee, how serious is this cat about music?” And some doctors, not knowing me, might wonder…

85.s: Carter was working to pay rent, not to hold the band together.
85.q: But I wasn’t frantically working to keep the orchestra together, although I certainly wanted to, but frantic is not a word for me. I was always looking forward and hoping better things would happen. But no, I was not frantically working to keep it together.

108.s: He felt lost after Lunceford died and recalls asking for a raise at 27.
108.q: There were times. I remember times, especially when Jimmie Lunceford died. I was very depressed at that time, because that orchestra was one that I was fond of, I was fond of him as a leader, and it was just beginning to get a response from the audience where the orchestra had begun to come…

555.t: Board of Education job and the insurance company
555.s: Tired of road conditions, she took the exam on her own, worked at the Board of Education and later an insurance company, with occasional gigs.
555.q: Nobody. I was good at math and all that, so I said, I’m through with this road business. I’m going to take – I think I took it on my own. I knew I was going to pass. There’s nothing new to me.

677.t: Special policeman and the plan to be a T-man
677.s: He was a special officer around 1929 and considered becoming a treasury agent.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Oh, yes. Yes, I was going to be a T-man, treasury agent, and I knew one-- and he came out here, and we talked, discussed the possibilities, and so I said, "Well, I'd like to do that." But I soon gave that up.

9.t: Taking a steady job with Great American Insurance
9.s: Because music wasn't steady he took an easy insurance job starting at noon, staying eighteen years until the company moved to California.
9.ch: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
9.q: : Well, this went on, yes. And that was one of the reasons I did get a steady job -- because the music wasn't steady. So I was talking to the wife: "Well, now, you're getting along in age now. It's time to start thinking about your old age." One of them kind of things. I said, "Yeah, I guess so."

231.t: Black entertainment in a wander; the tomato factory job
231.s: With salaries cut and his refusal to work for less, he sorted and delivered tomatoes in New York about 1947-49.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: I wonder what we should do with them. It was in a wander, man. Black entertainment was in a wander because of the fact that the axe that I guess that they had, were they too much in demand or not enough in demand. And they didn't know what to do with them. Because when they would cut salaries and I…

167.s: Rosenberg talks about his own short-order cook and bartending jobs.
167.ch: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
167.q: Yeah. The only thing you've got to do is watch that glass breaking in the place, you know.

0.t: Howard Scott leaves music for a day job
0.s: Scott drank heavily, took a day job as gig work slackened, and played society-type bands after Fletcher.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: Howard Scott? I don't think Scotty's too much older than me. I don't think he could be. I don't know. He might be around 73.

452.t: Selling insurance for Atlanta Life by day, playing with Larkin by night
452.s: After marrying in 1939 Cobb takes over his stepfather-in-law's insurance debit with Atlanta Life, working it while playing nights with Larkin.
452.q: Then I ended up with an automobile -- after I got married in 1939, writing writing insurance. How that came about, my stepfather-in-law, a man who was married to my wife's mother, had the biggest debit in the black insurance company here called Atlanta Life, whose home base is in Atlanta, Georgia.

641.t: New Orleans bricklayer-musicians and Standard Oil work in Baton Rouge
641.s: Fritz and Roque came from New Orleans to work as bricklayers at Standard Oil, where steady pay made music a sideline.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: Oh yeah, those guys... In fact... In the first place, they had no facilities. Fritz never went no place. And there wouldn't be no place in Baton Rouge for him to record.

566.t: Taking a job at the munitions plant
566.s: Thinking her career over, she drove elderly women to bingo. One drove her to a munitions plant and talked her into the hiring line, and she got the job after a doctor's check and a strike.
566.q: Yes. And at night time I used to take alot of the elderly ladies to the bingo games, you know. They'd call me and ask me if I'd drive them and I said, yes. So one day a lady wanted me to take her out to a place called The Bag Plant , it was munition's plant, you know, and so I said, "alright, I'll…

29.t: What Howard was doing then: cleaning, not playing
29.s: Howard says he was cleaning a basement and not playing at night then.
29.ch: Alma Hightower and other women musicians
29.q: Oh, What they had then, at that time, was anybody was just cleanin' up stores and things, that's--

6.t: Leaving Carter when the Arcadia closed; freelancing means laying off
6.s: He was with Carter only two or three months, then spent a period he jokes was called laying off, not freelancing.
6.ch: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
6.q: They'd say, "Hey, man, what are you doing?" "I'm not doing nothing now, I'm laying off." But then they'd say, "I'm freelancing," which was a dressed up word, meant the same thing, you were out of work.

115.t: The KKK Club and his many day jobs in Ottumwa
115.s: The band had the Klub Klee Klo gig and every other job in town; Gus worked in a furniture store, as a busboy and barber while sending money home.
115.q: Oh, sure, sure. I enjoyed that, you know. And we had a lot of fun. And we had all the jobs sewed up in this town, like, we worked at the club. The club was called KKK. Klub Klee Klo. But we called it the KKK Club, see.

124.s: Few musicians had day jobs; those who did worked in stores or elevators, while many lived off gigs.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: In the post office, your -- I don't think very few of them worked as a mailman because that was too hard a strenuous job.

76.t: Seven nights a week at the Nest
76.s: Zutty worked seven nights a week, slept all day, wore only a tuxedo, and he and Marge rarely got to a show or movie.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Yes, because that last (Unintelligible 1) worked every night. He worked there every night. Seven nights a week. Yes sir. Yes sir, he worked there seven nights a week.

171.t: Day job as assistant engineer at Western while playing nights
171.s: Married with a child, he took a $45-60 a month job at Western and played 8-to-4 clubs, napping in the boiler room.
171.ch: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
171.q: Those clubs on 12th Street-- they were 8 to 4, sometime 8 to 5. And those clubs--the man usually wouldn't let you quit. He wouldn't let me quit. And although I already had that job at Western University, I took the job in the music, you know, that steady job. But I'd gone with Todd in the winter of…
